title: The regional pitch: How football shaped modern Southeast Asian identity
content:
“I think we have turned a few doubters into believers, and that's nice ... what’s so heartening is you go back to the first leg and we were down 3-0, and Satu Nada (one heartbeat) was being sung,” said Lee. “As players, it is just amazing because that is the fuel, that's the belief that we can ride on and build on.”
One hearbeat in the stands
Lee’s reference to Satu Nada is particularly telling. Sung in Malay, the anthem is a staple at Jalan Besar and the National Stadium, echoing themes of unity, solidarity, and relentless passion.
What makes it truly special is its defiance, unlike fair-weather chants that fade when things go south, the ultras belt it out even when the Lions are trailing heavily, reminding the players they never fight alone. In a broader sense, it captures how football continues to foster a shared collective identity across Southeast Asia.
Football in Southeast Asia began not merely as recreation, but as an institutional battleground where colonized and modernizing societies negotiated sovereignty, identity, and civic coherence.
At its root, the sport was introduced across most of the region by Western powers as a by-product of colonization, a shared genesis for many modern Southeast Asian nations.
Even in Thailand, the region’s sole uncolonized state, football arrived via Siamese students returning from Britain in the late 19th century.
It quickly received royal patronage under King Vajiravudh (Rama VI, r. 1910–1925), becoming a cornerstone of state-led nationalism designed to project modernity and autonomy without falling under direct colonial rule.
Indonesia also holds a unique place in regional football history: playing under the name Dutch East Indies during the colonial era, it stands as the sole Southeast Asian representative in World Cup history, having featured at the 1938 finals in France.
As one of only three non-European entrants alongside Brazil and Cuba, the team’s campaign ended abruptly in the first round with a 6-0 loss to eventual finalists Hungary.
The squad that arrived on French soil was a vivid microcosm of the archipelago's complex social fabric. Predominantly indigenous, the team also drew talent from the colony’s Dutch and Chinese communities, bringing together players like goalkeeper Tan Mo Heng, Isaac Pattiwael, Franz Meeng, and captain Achmad Nawir.
These men were all amateurs who balanced football with their studies, civilian careers, and everyday livelihoods. In their multi-ethnic composition, this pioneering squad served as an early blueprint for modern Indonesian identity, prefiguring the pluralist ethos of Bhinneka Tunggal Ika ('Unity in Diversity') long before the nation achieved formal independence.
The introduction of football to French Indochina and British Malaya followed a remarkably similar trajectory: what began as an exclusive pastime for European colonizers was soon embraced by local populations, rapidly evolving into a popular grassroots phenomenon.
Football of the 'ASEAN 10' era
Throughout the Cold War, Southeast Asian football fractured along ideological fault lines. The ASEAN bloc maintained institutional continuity through the SEAP and SEA Games, while Indochinese nations were largely isolated from regional competitions, participating primarily in alternative anti-imperialist and socialist sporting networks.
The resolution of the Cambodian conflict through the 1991 Paris Peace Agreements and the subsequent accession of these nations into ASEAN (Vietnam in 1995, Laos in 1997, Cambodia in 1999) coincided almost exactly with their return to the regional pitch.
Across post-Cold War Southeast Asia, athletic re-engagement consistently outpaced diplomatic alignment, positioning football as an early bridge for regional integration. Vietnam's sporting return at the 1991 Manila SEA Games preceded its official accession to ASEAN by four years, functioning as an emotional pillar of the Đổi Mới transformation.
The momentum culminated in a silver-medal finish at the 1995 Chiang Mai Games and the hosting of the 1998 Tiger Cup. Anchored by 'Golden Generation' standouts such as Nguyen Hong Son and Le Huynh Duc, football provided a newly integrated populace with a shared civic identity that looked beyond historical conflict.
Similarly, Cambodia’s athletic re-emergence served as a harbinger of its return to the regional community. Having seen its sporting institutions and talent dismantled under the Khmer Rouge, the country's reappearance at the 1995 SEA Games after a two-decade hiatus, followed by the 1996 Tiger Cup, marked an essential step toward normalization, setting the stage for its formal entry into ASEAN four years later.
For Laos, rejoining regional competition served as a vital instrument of diplomatic visibility. Beginning with its return to SEA Games football in Singapore in 1993, four years prior to its 1997 ASEAN admission, and culminating in hosting the 2009 SEA Games in Vientiane, the country used the pitch to project international normalcy, cultivate civic solidarity, and weave deeper sporting ties with its maritime and mainland neighbors alike.
With the entry of Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia, Southeast Asian football completed its shift from a sub-regional Anglo-Malay and Thai sphere to a comprehensive pan-regional architecture.
Beyond institutional expansion, the resulting 'ASEAN 10' tournaments generated a recurring civic ritual of coexistence, translating abstract notions of regional community into a visible, affective reality far more effectively than state-level diplomatic summits.
The clearest evidence of an emerging Southeast Asian collective identity surfaces whenever the region’s teams step onto the continental stage, whether at the AFC Asian Cup, the AFC Champions League, or World Cup qualifiers.
While intra-regional rivalries remain fiercely contested, they quickly dissolve into cross-border solidarity whenever Southeast Asian teams face the wider world.
This spirit of 'ASEAN Pride' has been on full display time and again, from Vietnam’s fairytale run to the 2018 AFC U-23 final in Changzhou and Indonesia’s historic charge in the 2026 World Cup qualifiers, to standout continental campaigns by regional clubs. On each occasion, supporters across Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines have set domestic rivalries aside to rally behind their regional peers.
Confronting the athletic and economic hegemony of East Asian and West Asian powerhouses, from Japan and South Korea to Saudi Arabia and Iran, Southeast Asia functions as a cohesive sporting bloc. United by a collective underdog identity, its shared quest for parity and global recognition carries clear resonances of the region's anti-colonial past.
Unlike elite-driven diplomatic initiatives, this regional identity is built and sustained from the bottom up through everyday cultural rituals. Across national borders, public football fandom is remarkably uniform: the collective energy of nonton bareng (communal public screenings) in Indonesia mirrors the ecstatic đi bão ('storming the streets') celebrations in Vietnam and the bustling open-air screenings of Thailand.
Parallel to this street culture, digital media has woven millions of supporters into a single, highly interactive public sphere. Through vibrant online banter, cross-border league tracking, and mutual enthusiasm for ASEAN talent competing abroad, football has fostered an organic, lived sense of regional belonging that thrives well beyond the pitch.
As this week’s ASEAN Championship heads into its decisive clashes, reigniting storied rivalries like Malaysia versus Vietnam, with the prospect of an electric Vietnam–Thailand final on the horizon, the competitive drama will naturally command the headlines.
Yet beneath the tactical battles and tribal loyalties lies a deeper truth: football in Southeast Asia has never been solely about who lifts the trophy. Threaded through a century of shared colonial encounters, anti-imperial modernization, and vibrant grassroots terrace rituals, the game has quietly forged a collective regional identity that connects ordinary fans far beyond national borders.

title: Dopo un ictus i cani diventano alleati preziosi per i pazienti in riabilitazione
content:
Dopo un ictus i cani diventano alleati preziosi per i pazienti in riabilitazione
Indice
Spazzolare il pelo di un cane con la mano da riabilitare. Camminargli accanto lungo un corridoio. Lanciargli una pallina e recuperare, nel frattempo, un po’ di movimento. Alla Mayo Clinic alcune normali sedute di riabilitazione dopo un ictus sono state costruite intorno a queste attività. E i pazienti coinvolti si sono mossi di più, sono rimasti attivi più a lungo e hanno partecipato con maggiore coinvolgimento alla terapia rispetto a chi seguiva soltanto il programma standard. Lo mostra un trial randomizzato pubblicato su Mayo Clinic Proceedings.
Il risultato merita però una misura precisa. Lo studio riguarda 50 persone ricoverate dopo un ictus, seguite in un singolo programma ospedaliero, e mostra soprattutto un effetto sulla partecipazione e sull’attività durante le sedute. Non autorizza ancora a dire che un cane faccia recuperare più velocemente capacità motorie o autonomia nel lungo periodo. Su questo serviranno studi più grandi e un follow-up più lungo.
Il cane entra negli esercizi, non fa semplicemente compagnia
I ricercatori hanno assegnato casualmente i 50 pazienti a due gruppi. Il primo ha seguito la normale riabilitazione ospedaliera, che comprendeva fisioterapia, terapia occupazionale e logopedia. Nel secondo gruppo, composto da 25 persone, alcune sedute sono state svolte insieme a cani da terapia e ai loro conduttori. I partecipanti potevano effettuare da una a sei sessioni, della durata di 30 minuti ciascuna e distribuite nell’arco massimo di due settimane.
Un dettaglio cambia parecchio la lettura dello studio: le sessioni con i cani sostituivano alcune normali sedute riabilitative, non venivano semplicemente aggiunte aumentando le ore di terapia. La differenza osservata, quindi, non può essere liquidata con un banale “hanno fatto più esercizio perché sono rimasti più tempo in palestra”.
Il cane diventava parte dell’esercizio. Si poteva camminare al suo fianco, giocare al riporto, accarezzarlo o spazzolarlo, adattando l’attività agli obiettivi riabilitativi del singolo paziente. Un movimento ripetitivo resta un movimento ripetitivo; se alla sua estremità c’è un cane che aspetta la pallina, evidentemente può cambiare parecchio la voglia di farlo. La Mayo Clinic descrive proprio motivazione ridotta, poca energia, solitudine e scarso interesse per gli esercizi tra gli ostacoli che possono pesare sulla riabilitazione dopo un ictus.
Più partecipazione e più attività durante le sedute
La differenza più netta riguarda il coinvolgimento. I pazienti del gruppo con i cani hanno ottenuto punteggi significativamente più alti nella Pittsburgh Rehabilitation Participation Scale, utilizzata dai terapisti per valutare quanto una persona partecipa attivamente al trattamento. La differenza statistica tra i gruppi aveva un valore di p=0,0038.
Anche i sensori utilizzati per misurare il movimento hanno registrato più attività fisica per minuto nel gruppo con terapia assistita dal cane, con p=0,023, e una percentuale maggiore del tempo trascorsa in movimento, con p=0,006. È questo il dato concreto dietro l’idea dei pazienti che “camminano di più”: durante quelle sedute erano effettivamente più attivi e rimanevano mobili più a lungo.
Sono emerse anche differenze in due parametri della variabilità della frequenza cardiaca, utilizzata come indicatore della regolazione del sistema nervoso autonomo. Secondo gli autori, i cambiamenti osservati sono compatibili con una migliore risposta allo stress durante le sessioni. L’umore e gli altri parametri fisiologici misurati, compresa l’ossitocina salivare, non hanno invece mostrato differenze statisticamente significative tra i due gruppi. Il cane, insomma, non ha fatto miracoli ormonali: ha soprattutto reso i pazienti più partecipi e fisicamente attivi.
Lo studio è piccolo e non basta per parlare di recupero più rapido
Il campione resta ridotto. Nel solo gruppo sperimentale c’erano 25 persone, 17 uomini e 8 donne, con un’età media di circa 65 anni; 19 si sono identificate come bianche. Lo studio si è svolto alla Mayo Clinic di Rochester, in Minnesota, tra febbraio 2023 e febbraio 2024. Sono caratteristiche che restringono parecchio la possibilità di estendere automaticamente i risultati a tutti i pazienti colpiti da ictus.
Soprattutto, tra gli indicatori considerati dagli autori c’erano anche qualità della vita, umore e recupero funzionale, mentre gli effetti statisticamente più chiari pubblicati riguardano motivazione, partecipazione e quantità di movimento durante la riabilitazione. È una distinzione importante: essere più coinvolti nel trattamento è certamente interessante, ma rimane da verificare se sedute più frequenti o programmi più lunghi riescano a trasformare questo vantaggio in un recupero clinico maggiore nelle settimane e nei mesi successivi.
C’è inoltre un elemento da mettere sul tavolo insieme ai risultati: la ricerca è stata finanziata da Nestlé Purina PetCare Global Resources e condotta in collaborazione con l’azienda. Il finanziamento non invalida i dati, naturalmente, però appartiene alle informazioni necessarie per leggerli nella loro interezza e viene dichiarato dagli stessi autori.
E i cani come vivono queste sedute?
C’è anche l’altra metà della terapia, quella con quattro zampe. Lo stesso gruppo di ricerca aveva già pubblicato nel 2025 uno studio prospettico randomizzato sul benessere dei 14 cani da terapia con i rispettivi conduttori coinvolti nel programma di riabilitazione per l’ictus. Venivano controllati frequenza cardiaca, variabilità cardiaca, temperatura timpanica, cortisolo e ossitocina nella saliva, oltre ai comportamenti collegati allo stress.
Dopo le sessioni i cani mostravano una frequenza cardiaca più bassa e una maggiore variabilità cardiaca; cortisolo, ossitocina e comportamenti associati allo stress non presentavano variazioni significative. Gli autori hanno quindi concluso che, nelle condizioni studiate e con animali selezionati e conduttori qualificati, le attività non sembravano produrre uno stress misurabile nei cani. Alcuni parametri suggerivano persino uno stato di maggiore rilassamento.
È anche questo a distinguere un intervento strutturato dalla semplice idea di portare un cane in reparto sperando che faccia bene a tutti. Qui gli animali erano addestrati, lavoravano insieme ai loro conduttori e le attività venivano integrate negli obiettivi terapeutici.
Per ora il risultato più solido rimane molto concreto: durante alcune sedute di riabilitazione dopo un ictus, 50 pazienti sono bastati per osservare che la presenza di un cane può rendere il lavoro più coinvolgente e, soprattutto, far muovere di più chi deve ricominciare a farlo. Per sapere se quelle mezz’ore lasciano anche un segno più profondo sul recupero servirà il passo successivo della ricerca. Il cane, intanto, la pallina è già pronto a riportarla.
Fonte: Mayo Clinic Proceedings

title: From tropical forests to desert shores: Thailand and Qatar join hands on mangrove restoration
content:
Few would expect Thailand and Qatar to become partners in mangrove restoration. One is defined by its tropical coastlines and dense mangrove forests; the other by desert landscapes and the waters of the Arabian Gulf. Yet it is precisely this contrast that has created a remarkable opportunity for cooperation on environmental sustainability. That vision is now becoming a reality.
Through the facilitation of the Thai embassy in Doha, senior Qatari researchers recently undertook a five-day working visit to Thailand’s mangrove conservation sites, laying the groundwork for a mangrove restoration project in Qatar that will involve a Thai expert as a consultant later in 2026.
The visit was organised by the embassy in Doha in June, in cooperation with the Thailand International Cooperation Agency (TICA), Thailand’s principal agency for international development cooperation. The programme brought two senior researchers from Qatar University’s Environmental Science Centre (ESC) - Prof Dr Jassim al-Khayat and Prof Dr Vethamony Ponnumony - to visit Thailand’s coastal conservation sites, research centres, and government agencies responsible for marine and coastal resources.
According to the embassy, this visit marks the first major step toward deeper cooperation on sustainable development and mangrove restoration between Thailand and Qatar. This year, a mangrove expert from Thailand has been selected to serve as a consultant for a mangrove restoration project in Qatar, representing an important milestone in bilateral cooperation between the two countries in the field of sustainable development.
This progress did not happen by chance. For more than a year, the embassy in Doha has worked to position Thailand as a trusted partner for Qatar on environmental sustainability, laying the foundation for practical collaboration that benefits both countries.
The foundation for this initiative was laid in 2025 through two embassy-led visits by Thai experts to Qatar. The first visit was held from February 16 to 19, 2025, and included a seminar entitled 'Mangrove Conservation in Qatar: Towards a Practicable Action Plan', co-hosted with the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change (MECC), ESC, and Earthna Centre for a Sustainable Future on February 17, 2025 at Qatar Foundation.
The delegation also visited mangrove conservation sites, agricultural plantations, and eco-tourism locations in Al-Thakira and Al-Ruwais to observe conservation efforts, exchange expertise, and explore potential areas for collaboration. The second visit was held from April 22 to 23, 2025, and coincided with the Earthna Summit 2025, which the embassy, in collaboration with MECC, ESC, and Earthna, co-hosted a seminar entitled 'From Local to Global: Thailand’s Sustainability and Eco-Tourism Journeys', as an official side event of the summit.
The seminar highlighted Thailand’s sustainability frameworks, emphasising its globally recognised eco-tourism models, environmental conservation efforts, and community-driven development initiatives. The embassy also organised an exhibition at the Earthna Village 2025 to showcase Thailand’s journey towards sustainable development through the display of upcycled and community products from Thai mangrove forests, highlighting the achievements of community-driven development while demonstrating how local communities contribute to sustainable development.
The recent visit to Thailand in June brought the ESC delegation to meet with the institutions responsible for Thailand’s conservation ecosystem. In Phetchaburi Province on the western coast of the Gulf of Thailand, the delegation visited the Department of Marine and Coastal Resources’ Mangrove Resource Management Centre, observing mangrove nurseries and restoration techniques, as well as community-led value addition projects that generate sustainable livelihoods.
The group also visited the Laem Phak Bia Environmental Research and Development Project under Royal Initiative, a research centre recognised as a regional model for integrated coastal management and circular economy practices. In Chonburi Province on the eastern coast of the Gulf of Thailand, the delegation visited the Royal Thai Navy Sea Turtle Conservation Centre, where they explored an approach to marine animal conservation that engages public and military institutions with the private sector to protect endangered sea turtles and other marine species.
The visit also included policy discussions with senior representatives from TICA, the Department of Marine and Coastal Resources (DMCR), Kasetsart University, and the Royal Thai Navy. The discussions focused on exchanging knowledge about mangrove restoration protocols, marine resource conservation, and how ecotourism policy frameworks can be structured as conservation tools rather than as tools for resource exploitation.
The embassy noted that the visit delivered tangible outcomes, as both parties committed to strengthening institutional networks and academic cooperation. Although Thailand and Qatar face different environmental challenges, both countries share a common aspiration towards environmental conservation and sustainable development, a shared vision that underpins the growing partnership.
Thailand’s best practices in coastal resource management and mangrove conservation provide opportunities for academic cooperation with Qatar, which has already achieved remarkable progress in various environmental conservation and restoration projects under the Qatar National Vision 2030 and the Third National Development Strategy. Qatar brings considerable strengths to the partnership, namely strong institutional management and abundant natural resources that offer significant potential for conservation-led development. Against this backdrop, Thailand’s experience and expertise offer an accessible model that could be a beneficial addition to Qatar’s ongoing efforts.
As Thailand and Qatar continue to strengthen their partnership, the embassy said this initiative demonstrates how countries with vastly different environments can work together to address shared global challenges. What began as an exchange of expertise has evolved into a practical partnership - one that promises lasting benefits for environmental conservation, scientific cooperation, and sustainable development in both countries.

title: Homeless man becomes a superhero sign cleaner
content:
Homeless man becomes a superhero sign cleaner
- Published
A former homeless man has turned community superhero by cleaning dirty road signs across Surrey while dressed as Batman.
Liam Keen said he got the idea a few years ago after finding himself living in a van with his dog following a split from his partner.
He added that he set up his costumed community cleaning project as thanks for the support he was shown by the local Guildford community during that low point in his life.
"I decided the best way to pay them back for their kindness was to pay it forward," said Keen.
He explained that he ended up sleeping in a van with his dog Angel while dealing with a relationship breakdown and a chronic illness.
"It was winter time and I was really struggling - on top of which my dog decided to have herself five puppies," he said.
"I barely had enough money to keep the vehicle heated and put food on the table."
It was then that residents from Normandy, Ash and Ash Vale started to rally around, he added.
"Honestly, they blew me away with their offers of work and help with the dogs," he said. "They really got me back on my feet."
"So I'd go out every morning to pick up litter or clean graffiti and road signs.
"People got to hear about it and I ended up winning an award from the mayor for services to the community."
He added that the idea of dressing up as Batman came after he and his 'partner in grime' Dennis Rawlings - AKA Robin - were described as "superheroes" by one passerby.
"I'm just trying to repay a debt and make the place a bit better and brighter," said Keen.
"We wear the costumes to help draw attention to what we do, and besides, life's too short not to have a laugh."

title: AI flood map reveals 11 million Americans may be omitted from official risk zones
content:
Official flood maps shape disaster preparedness, insurance decisions and urban planning, but large parts of the United States remain unmapped or under-mapped. This means some communities may be left unaware of the risks they face, limiting their ability to prepare for future floods.
Researchers from the National University of Singapore (NUS) College of Design and Engineering (CDE) and Tsinghua University School of Architecture, led by Associate Professor Rudi Stouffs from the Department of Architecture at NUS, have co-developed a deep learning framework that completes missing and under-mapped flood hazard zones across the contiguous United States.
By learning from existing official flood records and terrain data, the framework generated a spatially complete 30-meter flood hazard map that reveals a much larger scale of flood exposure than current official maps indicate.
The paper, published in Nature Communications highlights the potential of AI to strengthen public access to flood risk information and guide more targeted resilience planning.
Revealing the scale of overlooked flood risks
The researchers found that official databases may have omitted around 11 million people and 4.1 million buildings from mapped flood zones. Taken together with the official baseline, the findings suggest that flood exposure across the contiguous United States may be substantially greater than currently recognized.
The study also found that these gaps are not evenly distributed. Many under-mapped and unmapped areas include socially vulnerable populations, particularly the elderly and children, pointing to wider implications for risk communication, resilience planning and the allocation of public resources to communities most in need.
That said, the research also showed that a concerted effort had been made to ensure more complete mapping in densely populated areas and economically weaker regions.
How the model completes patchy and inconsistent data
The framework was trained to learn the relationship between terrain features and known flood hazard zones. Using elevation data and existing official flood records, the model identified patterns associated with flood-prone areas and applied that understanding to places where flood mapping was incomplete or absent.
Researchers generated a continuous 30-meter flood hazard layer across the contiguous United States. The approach offers a scalable complement to conventional flood mapping, which can be costly and time-intensive.
A key strength of the AI model is its capacity to generalize the underlying relationship between modern terrain data and flood inundation patterns. Although trained on a noisy data set containing a mix of high-quality and outdated maps, the model learned to prioritize hydrologically consistent patterns over historical errors.
This capability is evident in its output. For instance, the model disregards the erroneous, abrupt boundaries found in some maps, which are often artifacts of administrative limits. Instead, it generates flood zones that logically follow the terrain.
In other cases, it extends the boundaries of underestimated flood regions to better reflect the topographical context. In areas lacking official maps entirely, the model can still produce credible flood risk assessments.
"The model functions as a robust validation and correction system. It does not simply replicate outdated information; it actively leverages current topographical data to produce flood maps that are more consistent and, in many cases, more accurate than the source material," said Stouffs.
"Our study shows that AI can do more than reproduce existing maps. It can help detect where flood risk has been missed, examine who may be affected, and uncover what kind of social impacts it may have," said Adjunct Associate Professor Ye Zhang from the Department of Architecture (and associate professor at Tsinghua University), a co-author of the paper.
"That creates an opportunity to improve public awareness of risk and its social implications and to support more strategic flood resilience efforts."
A public guide, not a replacement
While the researchers note that the AI-generated maps are not intended to replace official regulatory flood maps, they can serve as a public guide to highlight overlooked risk and support better targeting of future mapping and adaptation efforts.
"By making hidden risk more visible, this approach can help communities and decision-makers act earlier and plan more effectively," said Dr. Abraham Noah Wu, first author of the paper and formerly a doctoral student at the Department of Architecture and now a research fellow at Tsinghua University.

title: Assembly of giant wild sunflower family genomes unlocks potential for new perennial crops
content:
The Land Institute and HudsonAlpha Institute for Biotechnology, in collaboration with key partners, have assembled the first chromosome-scale, haplotype-phased genomes for Silphium integrifolium (rosinweed, silflower) and Silphium perfoliatum (cup plant, silphie). This landmark research promises to expand and accelerate the development of more climate-resilient, sustainable perennial crops.
These findings, published in the journal Nature Communications, provide foundational genomic data for domesticating wild, deep-rooted Silphium species native to North American prairies into perennial crops for food, fiber, forage and medicine.
Currently, more than half of the world's human calories come from just five crops: rice, wheat, corn, sugarcane and barley. Introducing perennial crops, such as Silphium species, that live for many years after planting could boost crop diversity and productivity while supporting long-term ecosystem health.
Highlighting the significance of this genomic milestone, David Van Tassel, lead scientist for the Perennial Oilseeds Program at The Land Institute, said: "Wild perennial species could help improve food security by contributing sustainability-enhancing traits such as deep roots. Genomics-informed breeding will help generate new crop varieties more quickly than in the past, but many wild perennials have challenging genomes. We showed that newer, affordable approaches work even for a stubborn genus that previously resisted genome assembly."
Key discoveries and impacts:
- Massive, complex genomes: The sequenced Silphium genomes are large—7.6 gigabases (Gb) for S. integrifolium and 7.5 Gb for S. perfoliatum. The individual chromosomes are among the largest known in plants. Researchers identified an unusual helical DNA structure that helps organize these giant chromosomes.
- Faster new crop development: By mapping genetic markers for traits like drought tolerance, heat adaptation and seed yield, breeders can now use genomic tools to rapidly domesticate Silphium while preserving its wild resilience.
- Sustainable oilseed crop: Silphium integrifolium is emerging as a promising, drought-tolerant perennial oilseed crop for food and medicine. Its seeds yield 11.8–25.3% edible oil and also contain squalene, which is valued for its use in vaccines and cosmetics.
- Ecological benefits: Silphium species support diverse prairie ecosystems and could also strengthen agricultural systems. Their roots, which reach depths of up to 4.5 meters (15 feet), help stabilize soil, increase organic carbon, improve water absorption and infiltration, and ensure resilience in drought conditions.
"Given the growing instability of climate patterns and disruptions in global food supplies, there's an urgent need to develop tools to accelerate domestication and breeding of more stress-resilient and locally adapted food crops," said Renan Souza, applied genomics researcher at The Land Institute and HudsonAlpha. "This genomic framework will help speed up the improvement of not only Silphium, but also other wild species with agricultural potential."
During the research, scientists created a method for DNA fingerprinting of individual plants. Breeders can use these fingerprints to make more accurate, faster selections, identifying which genes are important for disease resistance, larger seed heads and other key traits. Breeders can also use these fingerprints to identify and help conserve Silphium genetic diversity hotspots, which are key to studying how genetic and species diversity help regulate the spread of infectious diseases in prairies and perennial grain fields.
The next step for the authors is to scale up genotyping to enable fingerprinting thousands of plants each year, possibly by pooling efforts across institutions to achieve cost efficiency. The team will also follow up on the finding that several of Silphium's chromosomes are gigantic and may have an unusual structure. These genomic anomalies may need to be considered to optimize breeding and genetic conservation efforts.
Species in the genus Silphium range across the eastern and central prairies, grasslands and plains of the United States and southern Canada.
These ecosystems have evolved with grazing and burning and feature landscapes known and tended by numerous Indigenous communities, who have long-standing relationships with Silphium. The Land Institute researchers and collaborators are investigating the cultural dynamics of crop domestication and ethical approaches to data governance, including initial ethnobotanical research and engagement, development of educational materials and testing of participatory civic science methods.
The research was conducted by a diverse group of institutions, including The Land Institute, HudsonAlpha Institute for Biotechnology, University of Minnesota, Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, USDA ARS, University of Iowa, Savanna Institute, Saint Louis University, University of Georgia and Clemson University. Seeds for multiple local Silphium species and genotypes were donated by the Missouri Botanical Garden and the Southeastern Grasslands Institute.

title: Russia and Ukraine Release 20 Prisoners of War
content:
Ukraine and Russia exchanged 10 prisoners of war each, officials in Kyiv and Belarusian state media announced Monday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calling the swap a “special stage” of ongoing prisoner exchanges with Moscow.
Belarusian state media reported that Minsk mediated the latest release of servicemen held in captivity. Russia’s Defense Ministry did not immediately confirm the exchange.
On the Ukrainian side, two of the freed soldiers had been previously classified as missing in action since 2024 and eight since 2025, Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said.
The group included soldiers and sailors from the Ukrainian armed forces and national guard who had been fighting in eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
“Today, as part of a special stage of the exchange, we are bringing back 10 of our warriors — through Belarus,” Zelensky wrote on X. “It’s very important that we managed to bring them back.”
It was not immediately clear why Zelensky designated the swap on Monday as “special.”
The latest release of prisoners came less than a week after Russia and Ukraine each exchanged 103 servicemen following mediation from the United Arab Emirates.
At the time, Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko said that another exchange was expected before the end of the month.
Both Russia and Ukraine have released hundreds of prisoners of war since the start of the year through mediation from the United States and the UAE.
Repatriations of fallen soldiers and prisoner-of-war exchanges remain among the few channels of direct communication between Moscow and Kyiv since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

title: When glucose falls, ketone supplements may help protect the brain in type 1 diabetes
content:
Insulin is a cornerstone of treatment for patients with type 1 diabetes, essential for lowering blood glucose levels. However, if insulin doses are not appropriately matched to the body's needs, glucose levels can fall too low, resulting in hypoglycemia, a common and potentially dangerous complication of treatment. Hypoglycemia can impair thinking and cause symptoms ranging from dizziness and confusion to loss of consciousness.
New research from Yale, published in the journal Diabetes, identifies a potential new strategy for protecting the brain from the cognitive effects of hypoglycemia in people with type 1 diabetes.
The brain relies heavily on glucose as its primary source of fuel, explains Raimund Herzog, M.D., M.H.S., associate professor of medicine (endocrinology and metabolism) and senior author of the study. "When glucose falls below a certain threshold, the neurons in the brain stop working properly," he says.
"The easiest answer would be to take less insulin, but we know that higher glucose over the long term causes complications," Herzog adds. "The challenge is balancing good glucose control with the risk of hypoglycemia."
Ketones in a different context
Herzog and his team investigated whether ketones, molecules the body can use as an alternative source of energy, could protect the brain from the cognitive effects of low blood sugar. Specifically, the researchers focused on a ketone called beta-hydroxybutyrate.
"When patients with type 1 diabetes hear ketones, some of their alarm bells go off," says Herzog. Ketones are often a warning sign for patients with type 1 diabetes because they can indicate diabetic ketoacidosis, a potentially life-threatening complication of severe insulin deficiency. When the body lacks insulin, as is the case in untreated type 1 diabetes, it rapidly breaks down fat and produces ketones, which can accumulate to dangerous levels and make the blood acidic, explains Herzog.
However, Herzog and his team found benefits of ketones when they explored them in a different metabolic setting. Participants in the study continued to receive treatment with insulin, while dietary supplementation was used to modestly increase ketone levels as an additional source of fuel for the brain when glucose was low.
Memory held up during hypoglycemia
The study found that participants who received dietary supplementation to increase their ketone levels performed better on tests of working memory during hypoglycemia than those who received a standard diet, suggesting that increasing ketone availability may help preserve cognitive function when blood glucose is low.
The researchers believe this effect may be related to how the brain adapts to repeated episodes of low blood sugar. Previous studies have shown that recurrent hypoglycemia increases the brain's ability to transport certain alternative fuels, including ketones, across the blood-brain barrier. The findings suggest that dietary supplementation could take advantage of this adaptation, providing the brain with an alternative source of fuel when glucose is scarce.
A gap beyond diabetes tech
Herzog hopes these findings could eventually offer an additional layer of protection for patients who experience recurrent hypoglycemia, particularly those without access to technologies that continuously monitor glucose levels.
"Continuous glucose sensors and modern insulin pumps have made hypoglycemia much less frequent, but not everybody has access to that technology," says Herzog. "Globally, many patients still rely on insulin injections and fingersticks to measure their glucose, so hypoglycemia remains a significant risk."
Herzog also emphasized the collaborative nature of the research, which brought together expertise in endocrinology, neuroscience and brain imaging through longstanding partnerships with Yale's Magnetic Resonance Research Center. He believes this multidisciplinary approach will continue to drive advances in diabetes research.
"The goal of all of our studies is to help people achieve better glucose control without the associated hypoglycemia," says Herzog. "We're dedicated to finding a safe way for people to maintain that balance."

title: Amanal Petros: Vom Flüchtling zum Europameister
content:
Amanal Petros: Vom Flüchtling zum Europameister
18. August 2026Amanal Petros steht auf dem Victoria Square in Birmingham, die Deutschland-Fahne auf den Schultern, die Goldmedaille vor der Brust. Elf Monate nach dem hauchdünn verpassten WM-Titel in Tokio hat sich der 31-Jährige seinen ersten großen internationalen Titel gesichert.
Nach gut 25 Kilometern verschärft Petros an einer Steigung das Tempo und sprengt die Spitzengruppe. Keiner kann ihm folgen. Auf den letzten beiden Kilometern kann er den Sieg bereits genießen. Nach 2:09:11 Stunden läuft er ins Ziel - so schnell war noch kein Marathonläufer bei einer EM.
"Mein Ziel war, früh alles klar zu machen", sagte Petros. "Das hat super geklappt." Dass der Italiener Pietro Riva am Ende nur sieben Sekunden hinter ihm lag, spiegelte die Souveränität des Sieges kaum wider. "Ich hatte alles im Griff", freute sich Petros.
Erst einen Tag vor dem Rennen angekommen
Wegen Problemen bei der Einreise ins Vereinigte Königreich war Petros erst am Samstag, einen Tag vor dem Rennen, in Birmingham angekommen. Medienberichten zufolge gab es Schwierigkeiten mit seiner elektronischen Einreisegenehmigung. "Es hat sehr, sehr lange gedauert, es war furchtbar. Zwei Tage lang waren wir unterwegs, hin und her", erzählte er. Der Deutsche Leichtathletik-Verband half dabei, die Probleme zu klären.
Einen Tag später warteten acht Runden auf einem welligen Kurs mit Anstiegen und zahlreichen Kurven. Petros hatte sich monatelang in der Höhe von Kenia auf die EM vorbereitet. "120 Kurven, die Anstiege, eine Riesen-Herausforderung", gestand er. Aber die Vorbereitung habe sich ausgezahlt.
Die Strecke hinterließ trotzdem Spuren. "Es tut überall weh. Ich glaube, ich muss jetzt gleich zum Physio. Die Gelenke tun richtig weh", sagte Petros.
Sein EM-Gold widmete er seiner Mutter. "Sie ist meine Königin und mein Kraftspender", betonte Petros. "Wenn ich an sie denke, gibt mir das neue Energie und Motivation. Sie ist einfach die Beste."
Seine Mutter lebt mehr als 5000 Kilometer entfernt in der äthiopischen Region Tigray.
Mit 16 Jahren allein nach Deutschland
Petros wurde 1995 in der eritreischen Hafenstadt Assab geboren. Als kleines Kind floh er mit seiner Familie vor dem Krieg zwischen Eritrea und Äthiopien nach Tigray im Norden Äthiopiens. Dort wuchs er mit seinen beiden jüngeren Schwestern auf. Schon als Fünfjähriger arbeitete er auf dem Feld und kümmerte sich um Tiere.
Mit 16 Jahren verließ Petros Äthiopien allein. Anfang 2012 kam er nach Deutschland und wurde zunächst in Bielefeld als Asylbewerber untergebracht. Seine Mutter und seine Schwestern blieben in Tigray.
Ende 2021 hatte Petros wegen des Konflikts in der Region mehr als zwei Monaten keinen Kontakt zu ihnen. "Es ist sehr schwer", sagte er damals der DW. "Manchmal schlafe und träume ich sehr schlecht. Aber ich versuche, die Hoffnung nicht aufzugeben."
Das Laufen half ihm in dieser Zeit. "Wenn ich meinen Sport aufgeben würde, hätte ich alles verloren", sagte Petros der DW vor fünf Jahren. "Ich habe meine Familie schon verloren, und dann hätte ich auch noch das Letzte verloren, was ich gerade habe."
Die Situation in Tigray beschäftigte ihn auch während seiner Rennen. "Ich denke die ganze Zeit an meine Familie", sagte Petros 2021 der DW. Beim Laufen versuche er, die Gedanken auszublenden und sich auf den Sport zu konzentrieren.
Vom Fußball zum Marathon
Nach seiner Ankunft in Deutschland spielte Petros zunächst Fußball. Einem Betreuer fiel sein Lauftalent auf, er vermittelte ihn an einen Leichtathletikverein. Im Juni 2012, nur wenige Monate nach seiner Ankunft, bestritt Petros seinen ersten offiziellen Zehn-Kilometer-Lauf. Er gewann mit rund zweieinhalb Minuten Vorsprung.
Auch an das Leben in Deutschland musste er sich gewöhnen. "Die Sprache zu lernen, war eine große Herausforderung", sagte Petros damals der DW. "Aber eine noch größere war es, die deutsche Mentalität zu verstehen."
Bei seiner ersten Laufgruppe sorgte er gleich für Verwirrung. In Äthiopien sei es normal gewesen, auch unbekannte Menschen zur Begrüßung auf die Wange zu küssen, erzählte er damals. Also begrüßte Petros auch seine neuen deutschen Trainingspartner so. Die reagierten irritiert. Später verstand Petros, warum.
2015 erhielt er die deutsche Staatsbürgerschaft, später wurde er Sportsoldat. Seine Stärke lag zunächst auf den längeren Bahn- und Straßenstrecken, ehe er sich auf den Marathon konzentrierte. Bei den Olympischen Spielen 2021 in Japan lief er erstmals für Deutschland über die 42,195 Kilometer.
In den folgenden Jahren rückte Petros immer näher an die internationale Spitze. Im Dezember 2025 lief er in Valencia 2:04:03 Stunden und stellte damit den deutschen Marathonrekord auf. Im März 2026 folgte beim Berliner Halbmarathon in 59:22 Minuten ein weiterer deutscher Rekord.
Drei Hundertstelsekunden fehlten
Wie nah Petros inzwischen an der Weltspitze war, zeigte sich im September 2025 bei der Weltmeisterschaft in Tokio. 350 Meter vor dem Ziel zog er das Tempo an. Als Erster lief er ins Stadion und sah auf der Zielgeraden bereits wie der neue Weltmeister aus.
Doch der Tansanier Alphonce Simbu kam noch einmal heran. Petros schaute sich im Zielsprint zweimal um, Simbu schob sich auf den letzten Metern vorbei. Beide wurden mit 2:09:48 Stunden gemessen. Das Zielfoto entschied: 0,03 Sekunden fehlten Petros zu Gold.
"Das muss ich als Profi-Athlet einfach akzeptieren und nach vorne schauen", sagte Petros nach dem Rennen. Mit Silber gewann er die erste deutsche WM-Medaille im Marathon der Männer seit 1983.
Auch in Tokio sprach Petros über seine Mutter. Seit acht oder neun Jahren habe er sie nicht gesehen. Den Zieleinlauf habe sie nicht live verfolgen können. In ihrem Dorf gebe es weder Strom noch Internet, erzählte Petros.
"Für mich ist es eine riesengroße Geschichte, das zu erreichen. Besonders für meine Familie, für meine Mama", sagte er nach dem Rennen. Er wollte ihr Videos von seinem Lauf schicken. "Hoffentlich werde ich sie mal nach Deutschland zu einem Wettkampf bringen."
Diesmal kein Fotofinish
Jetzt, elf Monate nach dem verlorenen Fotofinish von Tokio, genoss Petros in Birmingham seinen ersten großen internationalen Titel. Nach WM-Silber 2025 und EM-Bronze im Halbmarathon 2024 stand er diesmal ganz oben auf dem Podest.
"Das Rennen war furchtbar, furchtbar schwer", resümierte Petros. "Aber mit ein bisschen Rotwein bin ich schnell wieder auf den Beinen."
Wie viel ein bisschen ist?
"Ach, so ein, zwei, drei Glas."

title: De campeón de la Copa Davis a convertirse de nuevo en futbolista: Roberto Bautista vuelve a los terrenos de juego tras colgar la raqueta

El castellonense se retiró de las pistas de este el pasado mes de julio tras disputar la Copa de España en Huelva.

El español ha retomado su carrera como jugador a la que renunció, curiosamente, por el tenis cuando apenas era un adolescente y ya ha debutado incluso con Els Ibarsos, equipo que actualmente milita en Primera FFCV.
El castellonense, héroe del equipo español que conquistó la Copa Davis en 2019 y semifinalista de Wimbledon ese mismo año, se retiró del tenis a principios de julio tras disputar la Copa de España en Huelva y puso fin a una carrera de dos décadas.

title: Tech is helping grocery stores waste less food. That’s a problem for food banks
content: First, the good news: Grocery stores are getting better at cutting food waste. AI tools can help better predict demand for each product, for example, and help a store reduce waste by more than a third. Other tech can help stores sell food before it expires. But there’s a catch—some food banks say that now they’re getting fewer donations. How retailers are getting better at wasting less Demand forecasting software is becoming widely used, with deep learning models that can predict how much of an item might sell based on everything from the weather forecast to the timing of food stamps. Afresh, one tool, is now in use in more than 12,000 grocery departments, and says that it has helped prevent more than 200 million pounds of food waste. Stores are less likely to overorder—in some cases, the AI handles ordering directly—and less food is thrown out. Guac, another AI ordering tool, says that its customers have been able to reduce food waste by as much as 38%. Another startup, Crisp, also forecasts demand to place orders, then uses artificial intelligence to better estimate shelf life, allowing retailers to intervene and change the price on produce, meat, or other perishable food so it sells before it goes bad. One study estimates that dynamic pricing can cut waste by 21%. Some apps also connect consumers with last-minute deals on food that’s about to expire at stores or restaurants. All of this can mean that less food is given away. Even as stores are becoming more efficient, more Americans are struggling to afford groceries and are more likely to go to food banks. “The food supply is tightening as the demand for [charitable] food is going up,” says Joseph Slater, chief operations officer at Gleaners Food Bank of Indiana. “What that has forced food banks into is to fill that gap, we have to buy food.” In 2018, the Indiana food bank spent most of its budget on infrastructure such as warehousing expenses, and since most of its food was donated, only 16% of charitable donations went directly to buying food. This year, 50% of its budget will go to buying food. Efficiency is increasing throughout the supply chain. Slater says meat producers that donated food to Gleaners in the past have slowed down production after having a surplus during the pandemic. They’ve also found new markets. Foods that are less demanded in the U.S., such as chicken drumsticks, are now being sold overseas rather than donated. Farmers are also using software to better predict demand when planting crops. But some of the changes are most noticeable at supermarkets, which historically have been the largest source of donated food for most food banks. In Washington, West Seattle Food Bank has seen a 10% drop in donations from the largest grocery stores it works with—a reduction of more than 15,000 pounds of food—over the past six years. Over the same period, the use of new efficiency tools has grown. “I worked in corporate grocery in 2017 and 2018 here in the Seattle area,” says Robbin Peterson, development director for the food bank. “And many stores, especially independents, were just starting to adopt the technology to do on-demand ordering.” In the past, she says, stores would keep around 10% extra stock to make sure they didn’t run out, but that’s not happening now. “I think that’s what we’re seeing—we’re not getting the fluff that they used to invest in to make sure that their shelf looks full,” she says. Other tools are also likely having an impact, like Too Good to Go, an app that helps stores and restaurants sell excess food at the last minute. “Those products are having an opportunity to be sold before they ever reach us,” Peterson says. The amount of donations fluctuates. West Seattle Food Bank recently had a surge in donations of lettuce and bagged salads—and anything labeled Taylor Farms—as people weren’t buying the produce at supermarkets because of cyclospora fears. (Some were wary at the food bank, too, Peterson says, although everything goes through multiple rounds of recall checks before it ends up there and is arguably even safer than buying at a retail store.) Some supermarkets also still reject truckloads of less-than-perfect-looking produce, some of which ends up at the food bank. The evidence is anecdotal so far, and in theory, a grocery store could reduce food waste in ways that don’t impact donations. For example, sensors and AI can track produce in storage to make sure it goes out on the sales floor before it goes bad—preventing waste without necessarily reducing the amount of edible food available to food banks. Still, the broader trend raises questions about whether greater efficiency could mean fewer donations. The Pacific Coast Food Waste Commitment, a coalition of businesses committed to reducing food waste, collectively cut its unsold food rate by 30% between 2019 and 2023. Total tons of unsold food also fell, while the percentage that was donated stayed roughly the same, meaning that food banks were ending up with less. Food banks are feeling the squeeze There are other reasons that food donations have fallen. The Trump administration has slashed funding for food aid. In 2025, for example, the U.S. Department of Agriculture cut $500 million that was supposed to be used to buy food for states to distribute to food banks, the equivalent of 94 million pounds of food aid. (The administration also cut funding that states could use to buy food from local farms.) “We’ve seen a trend over the last two years of our food donations going down by about 24%,” says Micah Crisman, a spokesperson for Manna FoodBank in North Carolina. “That’s been largely because of reductions in federal food support.” The food bank has faced other local challenges—like the fact that Hurricane Helene in 2024 destroyed grocery store and food distribution infrastructure. Individuals who might have donated food from their own pantries in the past are less likely to now because they’re also struggling with the higher cost of living, Crisman says. The organization has had to increase its purchasing budget by around 156% over two years. The problems are compounding. “At the time the supply chain was tightening, inflation was going up,” says Slater at Gleaners Food Bank. “Wages were stagnant, and it was putting more people in a position where they just weren’t able to meet kind of the basic household budgets, and that percentage of people continues to go up.” Millions of people, including many children, have already lost food aid after cuts to SNAP, the federal assistance program, and more changes to SNAP will roll out in October. The challenge is obviously larger than grocery stores adopting new technology: half of Americans now say they have trouble affording groceries, regardless of whether they have a job. Slightly older data shows that most households struggling to feed themselves have at least one adult working full-time. A system that forces people with jobs to rely on donated food is arguably broken. But in the economy we live in, food banks are critical. Some are finding creative ways to adapt as the landscape changes. In Indiana, Gleaners now aggregates demand from other food banks so that it can negotiate lower prices for the food it buys; it sells the food for a slight markup and uses that revenue to supplement its philanthropic dollars. It’s also started turning its own infrastructure into a business—for example, renting out storage space to food vendors who temporarily need more room. “That’s helped us locally fill the gap,” says Slater. “Truth be told, most food banks have not cracked that code and figured that out. They’re trying to. But it’s really important that we figure out how we earn money in addition to [raising money] to sustain this thing.”

title: Women’s physical and mental health 'inseparable', new endometreosis research finds
content:
in brief
- Almost half of women with endometriosis reported experiencing anxiety.
- One in three women experiencing mental health issues are not seeking help.
Women living with endometriosis, ovarian cysts and hormone-related conditions are experiencing significantly higher rates of anxiety, depression and self-harm, highlighting the need for mental health support to be integrated into women’s physical healthcare.
Research published by Women’s Mental Health Australia on Tuesday found almost half of women with endometriosis reported experiencing anxiety.
Women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome experienced depression and anxiety at up to twice the rate of women without the condition.
The findings have uncovered major gaps in Australia's healthcare system, according to chief operating officer Katrina Locandro.
"It's enormous," she told the Australian Associated Press.

"The government's investing a lot in women's health at the moment... and there is a really practical step that they could be taking to reduce that gap."
The findings indicate that physical health conditions are associated with poorer mental health.
But the greatest psychological toll is on women living with female-specific physical health conditions, including polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, a broad condition involving a hormone imbalance, irregular periods and ovarian cysts.
Women with that syndrome reported high rates of depression and anxiety, between 1.6 and 2.2 times higher than women who did not have the condition.
The disparity also extended to suicide and self-harm rates, reported by 10 per cent of women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome and 13 per cent of women with endometriosis, compared with four per cent of women without those conditions.
The research found that one in three women are not seeking help for their mental health issues, often because of financial and stigma-related reasons.
Locandro says every woman attending a government-funded endometriosis and pelvic pain clinic should receive an integrated mental health assessment and support as a standard offering.
"We're not asking the government to build a new system, we're asking it to strengthen an existing one by recognising that women's physical and mental health are inseparable," she said.
Report co-author Bronwyn Graham said that embedding integrated mental health assessment and support into existing services would be a game-changer.
"Women are being asked to manage two separate journeys, one for their body and one for their mind, and to find their own way between them at the point they are least able to."

title: Estas son todas las enfermedades de las que se vacunará a los migrantes en Ceuta
content:
Polio, difteria-tétanos, varicela, triple vírica...: las enfermedades de las que se vacunará a los migrantes en Ceuta
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
La medida busca garantizar la inmunización de aquellas personas que lo necesiten.
Ceuta recibirá hasta 45.000 dosis de vacunas procedentes de las comunidades autónomas y del Ministerio de Sanidad para reforzar la prevención frente a distintas enfermedades infecciosas. La Comisión de Salud Pública ha acordado activar el mecanismo de solidaridad entre territorios para enviar 45.000 dosis de vacunas: 15.000 dosis de la triple vírica, además de 10.000 de difteria-tétanos, y otras tantas de varicela y de polio a través del mecanismo de solidaridad para prevenir la transmisión de enfermedades tanto a la población ceutí no vacunada como a las personas migrantes.
La partida más numerosa será la de la triple vírica, una vacuna que protege frente a tres enfermedades: sarampión, rubéola y parotiditis o paperas. El sarampión es una enfermedad vírica extremadamente contagiosa que puede provocar fiebre alta, tos y una característica erupción cutánea y que, en algunos casos, deriva en complicaciones graves. La rubéola suele cursar de forma más leve, pero representa un riesgo especialmente importante durante el embarazo por las graves consecuencias que la infección puede tener para el feto. La parotiditis, popularmente conocida como paperas, es también una infección vírica y se caracteriza por la inflamación dolorosa de las glándulas salivales.
Entre las otras 10.000 dosis figuran las destinadas a proteger frente a difteria y tétanos, dos enfermedades bacterianas potencialmente graves. La difteria afecta principalmente a las vías respiratorias y puede generar complicaciones cardíacas y neurológicas. El tétanos, por su parte, no se transmite de persona a persona: la bacteria puede entrar en el organismo a través de heridas y producir una toxina que provoca rigidez y espasmos musculares intensos. La vacunación es la principal herramienta de prevención frente a ambas enfermedades.
También se enviarán vacunas contra la varicela, una infección causada por el virus varicela-zóster y muy contagiosa entre las personas susceptibles. Es especialmente conocida por la aparición de una erupción con vesículas acompañada habitualmente de picor y fiebre. Aunque en muchos niños evoluciona sin complicaciones importantes, la enfermedad puede presentar formas más graves, especialmente en adultos, embarazadas y personas con el sistema inmunitario debilitado.
La poliomielitis es otra de las enfermedades frente a las que se reforzará la protección. Está causada por el poliovirus y se transmite principalmente por vía fecal-oral. La mayoría de las infecciones pueden ser asintomáticas o leves, pero en una pequeña proporción de casos el virus invade el sistema nervioso y puede provocar parálisis irreversible. No existe un tratamiento que cure la poliomielitis, por lo que la vacunación resulta fundamental para prevenirla.

title: New initiative drives dramatic improvements in adolescent behavioral health screening
content:
A nationwide quality improvement initiative led by researchers and clinicians from UC Davis Health, the American Academy of Pediatrics and partner organizations resulted in significant increases in screening and follow-up care for adolescent substance use and mental health concerns across pediatric primary care clinics.
The findings are detailed in a study published in the American Journal of Medical Quality.
The Transformative and Evidence-based Approaches to Mental Health and Substance Use Screening (TEAMSS) collaborative engaged 160 clinicians at 27 pediatric primary care clinics across 18 states. The project aimed to strengthen screening, brief interventions and follow-up practices for adolescents ages 12 to 18 during routine health visits.
Researchers found substantial improvements over the 11-month initiative:
- Substance use screening increased from 35% to 75% of adolescent well visits.
- Follow-up care for adolescents with positive substance use screenings increased from 69% to 86%.
- Depression screening increased from 82% to 90%.
- Anxiety screening increased from 32% to 69%.
- Suicide risk screening increased from 18% to 41%.
"Adolescents are facing overlapping challenges related to substance use and mental health, yet these issues often go undetected in routine care," said Ulfat Shaikh, professor of pediatrics at UC Davis Health and lead author of the study.
"Our findings show that with the right support, coaching and evidence-based tools, primary care teams can dramatically improve screening and early intervention for young people."
Building sustainable systems for mental health and substance use screening
Mental health and substance use disorders frequently occur together and can worsen health outcomes if left untreated. National recommendations encourage routine screening, but implementation has often been limited by time constraints, lack of standardized workflows and insufficient resources.
To address these barriers, TEAMSS adapted the Institute for Healthcare Improvement's learning collaborative model for a virtual environment. Participating clinics received training, coaching, peer-to-peer learning opportunities, data feedback and practical tools to improve clinical workflows and adopt validated screening instruments.
Clinics implemented a range of evidence-based strategies, including:
- Standardized screening protocols.
- Use of validated screening tools such as CRAFFT, PHQ-9, GAD-7 and Ask Suicide-Screening Questions.
- Integration of screening into electronic health records.
- Mobile device-based screening workflows.
- Expanded involvement of interdisciplinary care teams.
- Development of community partnerships and referral networks.
More than 90% of participating clinicians reported that TEAMSS improved or significantly improved patient care and clinic operations. Nine months after the collaborative ended, 85% of clinics reported they had fully maintained the changes implemented during the project.
"Our virtual model allowed clinics across the country to participate regardless of geography," Shaikh said. "The combination of brief learning sessions, individualized coaching and peer learning helped practices build sustainable systems for addressing adolescent behavioral health concerns."
The researchers noted that while improvements in screening were substantial, future efforts should focus on expanding suicide risk screening, strengthening community partnerships and supporting resource-limited and rural clinics.
The study concludes that virtual learning collaboratives can serve as an effective, scalable approach for improving adolescent behavioral health screening and care delivery in primary care settings.
"One of my biggest takeaways from the TEAMSS project is that busy primary care clinics are eager to improve mental health and substance use care for adolescents when they have practical tools, peer support and opportunities to learn from one another," Shaikh said.
"I am deeply grateful to the clinics, clinicians and staff who participated in this work despite competing demands on their time," she added. "Their commitment to learning and improvement made this project successful and ultimately helps create better care for adolescents and their families."

Até ao fim de agosto, estarão entregues 28.000 novas casas públicas, anunciou o Governo neste sábado, ultrapassando-se assim as metas estabelecidas no âmbito do Plano de Recuperação e Resiliência (PRR).

A informação, que foi avançada na sexta-feira por Luís Montenegro na festa partidária do PSD, no Pontal, surge num comunicado conjunto dos ministérios da Economia e da Coesão Territorial e das Infraestruturas e Habitação. Segundo estes, a meta de 26.000 casas, definida no âmbito do PRR, através do 1.º Direito – Programa de Apoio ao Acesso à Habitação, “mais do que cumprida, será ultrapassada”, com a entrega, até ao final de agosto, de mais de 28.000 habitações públicas localizadas em todo o país.
Além destas, mais 12.000 habitações “estão em obra avançada, prevendo-se que, até dezembro de 2026, seja possível concretizar um total de 40.000 casas”, acrescentaram os dois ministérios.
Segundo o executivo, o cumprimento desta meta foi possível através de “um conjunto de medidas previstas no programa Construir Portugal, para desbloquear e acelerar processos”, e da “estreita colaboração entre o Governo, o Instituto da Habitação e Reabilitação Urbana (IHRU) e os municípios”.
Para o cumprimento da meta, as verbas do 1.º Direito foram reforçadas em 2.800 milhões de euros (ME), através do Orçamento do Estado, que se somaram aos 1.400 ME dos fundos do PRR, “que se revelaram insuficientes”, acrescentaram os dois ministérios.
No comunicado, acrescentaram que, a estas respostas habitacionais do âmbito do PRR, irão somar-se, até 2030, cerca de 12.000 habitações para arrendamento acessível e a concretização das Estratégias Locais de Habitação, nas quais os municípios identificaram a necessidade de cerca de 133.000 fogos habitacionais.
Segundo o Governo, até 2030 serão mobilizados cerca de nove mil milhões (ME) de euros para habitação pública.

title: Aeropuerto de Maiquetía retomará operaciones en terminales temporales a partir del 1º de septiembre
content:
El Instituto Aeropuerto Internacional de Maiquetía (IAIM) informó que a partir del martes 1º de septiembre de 2026 comenzarán formalmente las operaciones en los terminales temporales habilitados para atender vuelos nacionales e internacionales.
A través de un comunicado publicado este martes 25 de agosto, el organismo señaló que la apertura de estas instalaciones forma parte del proceso de reconstrucción del aeropuerto, que, según indicó, se desarrolla bajo estándares de calidad y con nuevas soluciones tecnológicas.
El aeropuerto destacó que los terminales temporales permitirán mantener la conectividad aérea mientras avanzan las labores de recuperación de la infraestructura aeroportuaria. El organismo presentó la reapertura como parte de un proceso de reconstrucción que busca recuperar progresivamente las operaciones del principal aeropuerto del país.
¿Qué deben hacer los pasajeros?
Ante el inicio de las operaciones en los terminales temporales, el Aeropuerto de Maiquetía recomendó a los pasajeros comunicarse directamente con sus respectivas aerolíneas para verificar la reprogramación de sus vuelos y confirmar hacia cuál terminal deberán dirigirse.
El instituto también pidió a los viajeros mantenerse atentos a sus redes sociales y canales oficiales, donde serán publicados próximos anuncios y actualizaciones relacionadas con el funcionamiento de las instalaciones.
El comunicado no detalla cuáles aerolíneas operarán desde cada terminal ni especifica el itinerario de vuelos que será trasladado a las instalaciones temporales. Estos datos deberán ser confirmados directamente por las compañías aéreas.
Cómo funcionarán los terminales temporales en el Aeropuerto de Maiquetía
La infraestructura provisional estará conformada por dos terminales para las salidas y dos para las llegadas, con espacios para pasajeros de vuelos nacionales e internacionales.
Avanzamos a paso firme para la próxima reapertura de las puertas de Venezuela🌎
— Aeropuerto Internacional de Maiquetía (@IAIM_VE) August 22, 2026
Te esperamos en #Maiquetía con espacios diseñados para el restablecimiento progresivo de nuestras operaciones de forma cómoda, moderna y segura✈️ pic.twitter.com/ode2ulAviD
El terminal nacional de salidas tendrá una superficie de más de 3.300 metros cuadrados, tres puertas de embarque y capacidad para atender hasta 480 pasajeros simultáneamente.
Por su parte, el terminal internacional de salidas contará con unos 4.300 metros cuadrados, cuatro puertas de embarque y capacidad para 780 pasajeros en sus salas de espera.
Para las llegadas, se habilitará una estructura de aproximadamente 2.550 metros cuadrados, dividida para recibir vuelos nacionales e internacionales. A esta se sumará una instalación adyacente de 1.000 metros cuadrados destinada a la espera de pasajeros.
¿Qué tendrán los terminales temporales?
De acuerdo con la información difundida por el IAIM, las estructuras estarán construidas con módulos de metal reforzado, cerramientos interiores de drywall y revestimientos exteriores de policarbonato. Los techos serán de aluminio y estarán integrados con lonas de alta resistencia.
Asimismo, las instalaciones dispondrán de los principales servicios para la atención de los viajeros, entre ellos:
- Controles aeroportuarios
- Salas de espera
- Aire acondicionado
- Baños
- Servicio médico
- Wifi gratuito e ilimitado
- Estaciones de carga para dispositivos electrónicos
- Máquinas expendedoras de alimentos y bebidas
El aeropuerto también aseguró que contará con asistencia para personas con movilidad reducida durante todo el recorrido, mientras que los pasajeros podrán viajar con mascotas, siempre que cumplan con la normativa vigente.
Dos meses cerrado
El Aeropuerto de Maiquetía permanecía cerrado desde el 24 de junio, luego de que las autoridades suspendieron las actividades para evaluar y reparar los daños.
Posteriormente se estableció un plan de recuperación por fases que contempla la utilización de infraestructura temporal para recuperar parcialmente la conectividad aérea.
Durante agosto se realizaron además pruebas y simulacros operativos en las nuevas instalaciones. El objetivo era evaluar los procedimientos de chequeo, embarque, manejo de equipaje y circulación de pasajeros antes del regreso de las operaciones comerciales.
Distribución actual de las operaciones
Actualmente, el Aeropuerto Internacional Arturo Michelena de Valencia (Carabobo) tiene la mayor carga operativa con 65 frecuencias semanales, al servir de base para compañías europeas como Iberia y Plus Ultra, además de las operaciones continuas de Copa Airlines.
Por su parte, el Aeropuerto Internacional La Chinita de Maracaibo (Zulia) mantiene 24 vuelos semanales, dentro de los cuales figura la ruta diaria operada por American Airlines hacia la ciudad de Miami, una planificación comercial que la empresa aérea había estructurado previamente al desastre natural.
En el caso del Aeropuerto Internacional José Antonio Anzoátegui de Barcelona (Anzoátegui), líneas aéreas como Laser han establecido rutas especiales para mantener enlaces internacionales, que incluyen trayectos hacia Madrid, debido a las limitaciones de espacio presentes en el terminal de Valencia.

title: Syria's Kurdish-led SDF dissolves as part of integration with Damascus
content:
Syria's Kurdish-led SDF dissolves as part of integration with Damascus
DAMASCUS, Aug 25 (Reuters) - The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces has been dissolved, the armed militant group's leader said on Tuesday, a major step in the integration plan agreed on earlier this year with the Islamist-led government in Damascus.
"We announce today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and announce with full responsibility its dissolution as an independent military force," SDF commander Mazloum Abdi said in a televised speech.
The government and the group, which helped defeat the Islamic State with U.S. backing and held parts of northern and eastern Syria, agreed in January to a phased integration of Kurdish fighters into the state, a plan Washington called a "historic milestone".
The deal came shortly after government forces under President Ahmed al-Sharaa launched a lightning offensive in January, taking swathes of the areas the SDF held.
Abdi said that the announcement followed an agreement with Sharaa after the integration of the group's forces into the army.
The Kurdish People's Protection Units, which formed the core of the SDF, had already been integrated within state forces with its commander, Sipan Hamo, appointed in March deputy defence minister for the country's eastern territories.
The SDF dissolution comes as the new leaders in Damascus seek to resolve internal strife and rebuild Syria, with support from Washington, after nearly 14 years of civil war and decades of isolation under former President Bashar al-Assad's rule.
(Reporting by Orhan Qereman and Nayera Abdallah, Writing by Nayera Abdallah; Editing by Alistair Bell)
